name: Multilingual LibriSpeech (MLS)
description: A large-scale multilingual corpus suitable for speech research, derived from read audiobooks from LibriVox and consisting of 8 languages, including about 44.5K hours of English and a total of about 6K hours for other languages. The paper also provides language models and baseline ASR models for all languages.
creator: Vineel Pratap, Qiantong Xu, Anuroop Sriram, Gabriel Synnaeve, Ronan Collobert
inLanguage: English, German, Dutch, Spanish, French, Portuguese, Italian, Polish
citeAs: Vineel Pratap, Qiantong Xu, Anuroop Sriram, Gabriel Synnaeve, Ronan Collobert. MLS: A Large-Scale Multilingual Dataset for Speech Research. December 22, 2020.
rai:dataCollection: The dataset was created from LibriVox audiobook data and corresponding text sources. The authors selected 8 languages based on audiobook hours and text availability, downloaded audiobooks using LibriLight tools, downsampled audio from 48kHz to 16kHz, segmented long audio files into 10-20 second segments using acoustic models and silence intervals, generated pseudo-labels with beam-search decoding and 4-gram language models, downloaded or manually retrieved source texts from multiple domains, normalized text, retrieved transcripts by matching pseudo-labels to source text using TF-IDF and Smith-Waterman alignment, filtered candidate transcripts with WER greater than 40%, and created train, development, and test splits with no speaker overlap.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web API, Software Collection, Document analysis, Manual Human Curator
rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The training data is lower than the available audiobook data because the text source for some audiobooks may not have been downloaded, candidate labels may have been filtered during transcript retrieval, or data may have been filtered while creating validation/test splits.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consists of read-speech audiobooks from LibriVox and corresponding book text sources from domains including gutenberg.org, archive.org, ccel.org, hathitrust.org, and other language-specific websites. For language model data, source text was taken from Project Gutenberg books.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Audio was segmented into 10-20 second utterances by running inference to obtain token timestamps and splitting at the midpoint of the longest silence between 10 and 20 seconds, or at 20 seconds if no silence was found. Source text was split into overlapping 1250-word documents with stride 1000. Candidate transcripts were retrieved using TF-IDF similarity on bigrams and Smith-Waterman alignment, then filtered if WER with pseudo-labels exceeded 40%. Numbers in matched text were replaced with aligned words from pseudo-labels, and heuristics were applied to hyphens and apostrophes.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Audio data was downsampled from 48kHz to 16kHz. Text normalization included NFKC normalization, removal of unwanted characters such as punctuation, subscript/superscripts, emojis, and escape symbols, removal of end-of-line hyphenation and joining split words, and filtering characters outside a valid unicode character list based on each language's orthography. Books with corrupted metadata, missing title, missing speaker/author information, multiple speakers, or duplicate versions were removed. Chapters were constrained to appear in only one partition.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Transcripts were created automatically by generating pseudo-labels for segmented audio with acoustic models and 4-gram language models, then matching these pseudo-labels to original book text. For high-quality development and test sets, human transcribers listened to the audio while viewing the transcript and corrected only clear and obvious errors.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Candidate transcripts were filtered out if the WER between the candidate transcript and pseudo-label was greater than 40%. For development and test sets, transcript quality was assessed by human verification, and the paper reports WER between generated transcripts and human rated transcripts for each language.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: wav2letter@anywhere, acoustic models using Time-Depth Separable Convolutions with ASG loss, beam-search decoding with 4-gram language models, TF-IDF similarity scoring, Smith-Waterman alignment, pdftotext, gender classifier based on SVM with RBF kernel, KenLM
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset will be made freely available for anyone at http://www.openslr.org. The paper also states that pretrained models and recipes will be made available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/wav2letter. No updating timeframe or deprecation policy is specified.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Speaker gender was labeled for all speakers with a gender classifier and used to balance development and test sets. Speaker information was also used to avoid overlap across splits.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The authors state that they believe the dataset will open new avenues in ASR and Text-To-Speech research and promote open research in large-scale training of ASR systems and multilingual ASR.
rai:dataBiases: To avoid potential bias from human transcribing during verification of development and test sets, transcribers were asked to correct only clear and obvious errors.
rai:dataLimitations: The dataset covers 8 languages selected based on audiobook hours and text availability. For non-English languages, automatic extraction of text sources was challenging due to diverse domains and invalid links, requiring manual approaches. Transcript retrieval is imperfect because pseudo-labels may not always have the correct transcription of the audio. Numbers are challenging to normalize generically. Polish language model decoding is negatively impacted by a 13% OOV rate. The training data is reduced because some text sources were unavailable, some candidate labels were filtered, and some data was excluded during split creation.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for speech research, especially Automatic Speech Recognition and Text-To-Speech research. It provides train, development, and test splits, as well as limited supervision subsets of 10 hours, 1 hour, and six 10-minute sets for low-resource training benchmarks. It also includes language model training data and pre-built language models.
